Scientific studies have demonstrated that UVC light can reduce viral loads on surfaces such as glass and stainless steel by over 99% after just a few seconds of exposure, and UVC lighting systems installed in HVAC units have been found to significantly lower the viral load in indoor air [1]. These findings indicate that UV light, when properly applied, can be an effective disinfection tool to reduce the presence of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, in public and private spaces [1]. However, it is important to note that UVC light is hazardous to human skin and eyes, so safety measures must be strictly followed when deploying UV disinfection systems [1]. Properly shielded UVC fixtures can be safely used in occupied spaces to minimize human exposure while effectively reducing pathogens [1]. Experts from organizations such as the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have expressed optimism about the potential of UV light to help prevent virus transmission, especially in high-density public environments, provided that correct protocols are in place [1]. In summary, while direct exposure to UV light is not a practical or safe method for individuals to prevent COVID-19 infection, the use of UVC light in controlled and shielded disinfection systems can significantly reduce the presence of the virus in the environment and thus contribute to COVID-19 prevention efforts [1]. More research and regulatory guidance are needed to ensure the safe and effective implementation of this technology [1].
